text: Which pieces of information surfaced during the discussion and which weren’t? What explains the pattern of information sharing? For example, information regarding the wealth of richer citizens is only held by those individuals and they often keep it to themselves unless they are pressed by others. In addition, while citizens largely expect the merchants to be rich and so often press them for details about their wealth, citizens don’t always expect the mayors to be rich and so mayors typically have more leeway for making a choice regarding sharing information about their wealth.

Some of the distributed information is useful (such as the masons’ ability to cooperate to lower costs) while other parts of it is not (rumors about corruption that are not accompanied with any evidence). Which pieces of information surfaced? Which of these pieces of information received more attention and care? What can explain the pattern?
How much attention was given to the fact that some citizens had more information than others? Does quantity of information relate to quality of information?
How much attention was given to the disagreement between the information given to different participants?

How were the interests of citizens shared and considered? Were they equally considered? Was there a clear tally of who supports which goal? Were there assumptions being made about others? Were some interests considered more legitimate than others?
How did the rules of discussion - the need to pass legislation, the randomly selected moderators, the tradition of giving space to mayors - affected the choices made?
What decisions were made by the group? How were they worded? What are the implications of the way they were worded and the content of the decisions?
Oftentimes students would ‘grade’ themselves and say that they did a good job or made a good collective decision. How should such collective decisions be evaluated?

Were the especially good examples of constructive disagreement skills? E.g. students reflecting to others what they heard they said, finding constructive agreements, identifying points of disagreement productively etc.
Are there examples of unproductive engagement? Mocking other people’s opinions, personal attacks, uncharitable interpretations etc.

What moral values motivated students in their decision making? Can they articulate them? Can they explain why they did or didn’t behave in accordance with some moral values? (is it because they don’t hold these or did something else win out?)
outcome: Face trade-offs between moral values and strategic goals
